sources.title: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed.
sources.locator: Contents (PDF pp. 4-5) naming §§2.2 and 3.2; §2.2 Weak Laws of Large Numbers, including §§2.2.1-2.2.3 (printed pp. 56-66; PDF pp. 63-73); and §3.2 Weak Convergence, including §§3.2.1-3.2.2 and Exercises 3.2.1-3.2.12 (printed pp. 116-124; PDF pp. 123-132), all read in the full 490-page PDF.

contents.name: 2.2 Weak Laws of Large Numbers (definition of convergence in probability)
Theorem 2.2.1 (variance of a sum of uncorrelated variables)
contents.reason: This variance computation belongs with weak laws of sums, where the uncorrelated-variable hypotheses and applications are developed rather than merely used as a convergence-mode instance.

contents.name: Lemma 2.2.2 (vanishing L^p moment implies convergence in probability)
Example 2.2.4 Polynomial approximation
contents.reason: The Bernstein-polynomial approximation is an analysis application of a weak law and does not provide a reusable random-variable convergence-mode claim for this pair.

contents.name: Example 2.2.5 A high-dimensional cube is almost the boundary of a ball
contents.reason: This geometric concentration application uses a weak law but develops high-dimensional volume intuition rather than the definitions or implications selected for this modes page.

contents.name: 2.2.2 Triangular Arrays
contents.reason: Triangular-array weak laws are a later law-of-large-numbers branch; this page needs only the general convergence-in-probability language in which their conclusions are stated.

contents.name: Theorem 2.2.6 (variance criterion for convergence in probability)
contents.reason: The theorem is a normalization criterion for random sums, so its hypotheses and applications belong with weak laws rather than the abstract implication diagram.

contents.name: Example 2.2.7 Coupon collector's problem
contents.reason: The coupon-collector normalization is a concrete triangular-array weak law and is assigned to the planned page whose purpose is to develop weak-law applications.

contents.name: Example 2.2.8 Random permutations
contents.reason: The random-permutation cycle calculation is a combinatorial application of weak-law estimates and would introduce an unrelated model into a general convergence-modes pair.

contents.name: Lemma 2.2.9 (independence of random-permutation cycle indicators)
contents.reason: This lemma serves the preceding random-permutation example only; it is neither a general mode-of-convergence fact nor a prerequisite for an item in this scaffold.

contents.name: Example 2.2.10 An occupancy problem
contents.reason: The occupancy asymptotic is a model-specific weak-law application and is deliberately not added merely to furnish another example of convergence in probability.

contents.name: 2.2.3 Truncation
contents.reason: The section develops truncation for weak laws of sums; the uniform-integrability theorem here has a different finite-measure role through the published Vitali theorem.

contents.name: Theorem 2.2.11 Weak law for triangular arrays
contents.reason: This central triangular-array weak law requires its own array notation and truncation setup, which the planned weak-laws page is designed to introduce.

contents.name: Theorem 2.2.12 Weak law of large numbers
contents.reason: The iid tail criterion is a substantive weak-law result, not an implication among modes, and the plan assigns it to the later weak-laws-and-series development.

contents.name: Remark after Theorem 2.2.12 (necessity of the centering criterion)
contents.reason: The centering necessity refines the theorem's weak-law content and must remain adjacent to the iid tail criterion that the later weak-laws page will establish.

contents.name: Remark after Lemma 2.2.13 (subcritical moment consequence)
contents.reason: The comparison between the tail condition and subcritical moments is a qualification of the later iid weak-law criterion, not a new convergence-mode implication.

contents.name: Theorem 2.2.14 (iid integrable weak law)
contents.reason: The familiar iid integrable weak law is a destination result for the weak-laws page, whose proof will use this pair's convergence-in-probability definition.

contents.name: Example 2.2.15 (Cauchy variables and failure of a weak law)
contents.reason: This failure concerns centering of iid averages under heavy tails, so it belongs alongside the tail criterion rather than as a counterexample to a generic mode implication.

contents.name: Example 2.2.16 The St. Petersburg paradox
contents.reason: The infinite-mean normalization calculation is a weak-law application with specialized heavy-tail content, reserved for the planned weak-laws and series page.

contents.name: 3.2.1 Examples
contents.reason: This examples section studies weak limits themselves; the present page records only the real-line definition and relations between modes, leaving weak-limit examples to PT-7.

contents.name: Example 3.2.1 (De Moivre-Laplace weak convergence)
contents.reason: This normal-limit calculation is a central-limit theorem application, so it belongs at the later planned central-limit page rather than in the foundational modes pair.

contents.name: Example 3.2.2 (Glivenko-Cantelli empirical distribution functions)
contents.reason: Empirical-distribution convergence is a weak-convergence example with its own probabilistic setting, reserved for the later weak-convergence treatment.

contents.name: Example 3.2.4 Waiting for rare events
contents.reason: The geometric-to-exponential scaling limit is a weak-limit example and is not needed to establish the abstract implication and counterexample map on this page.

contents.name: Example 3.2.5 Birthday problem
contents.reason: The birthday-problem scaling calculation is a model-specific probability application, not a general relationship between convergence in probability, L^p, almost sure, and distribution.

contents.name: Example 3.2.6 (central order statistic)
contents.reason: This order-statistic asymptotic requires a separate sampling model and density calculation, neither of which is required by the self-contained modes-of-convergence route.

contents.name: Lemma 3.2.7 (density of the central order statistic)
contents.reason: The density lemma is solely an ingredient of the preceding order-statistic example and would be an unsupported detour from the general convergence framework.

contents.name: 3.2.2 Theory
contents.reason: The theory section develops the general weak-convergence machinery that the plan explicitly allocates to PT-7 after this real-variable introductory page.

contents.name: Theorem 3.2.8 (quantile coupling / almost-sure representation)
contents.reason: This representation theorem is a weak-convergence construction; it is deliberately postponed to PT-7 rather than used to short-circuit the direct proofs selected here.

contents.name: Theorem 3.2.9 (bounded-continuous-function characterization)
contents.reason: The bounded-continuous test-function characterization is part of the planned weak-convergence toolkit and exceeds the CDF-based real-line definition fixed for this page.

contents.name: Theorem 3.2.10 Continuous mapping theorem
contents.reason: This is the distributional continuous-mapping theorem; this scaffold instead proves its distinct convergence-in-probability counterpart without forward-citing PT-7.

contents.name: Remark after Theorem 3.2.10 (measurability of the discontinuity set)
contents.reason: The Borel-status observation serves the distributional continuous-mapping theorem and is therefore carried with that PT-7 theorem rather than duplicated for probability convergence.

contents.name: Theorem 3.2.11 (Portmanteau equivalences)
contents.reason: Portmanteau open, closed, and continuity-set formulations are the centerpiece of the later weak-convergence page, not a prerequisite for this CDF-level introduction.

contents.name: Remark after Theorem 3.2.11 (open-set boundary example)
contents.reason: The boundary example explains the Portmanteau inequality directions, so it belongs with the later theorem rather than supplying an unrelated B-page counterexample.

contents.name: Theorem 3.2.12 Helly's selection theorem
contents.reason: Helly selection addresses subsequences of distribution functions and possible mass loss, material specifically scheduled with tightness in the future PT-7 page.

contents.name: Remark after Theorem 3.2.12 (mass escape and vague convergence)
contents.reason: The mass-escape example introduces vague convergence, which is a central topic of the future tightness-and-representation page and is not part of this CDF-level scope.

contents.name: Theorem 3.2.13 (tightness and probability-valued subsequential limits)
contents.reason: The tightness criterion is a named future topic in PT-7 and is intentionally not assumed in the direct real-variable Slutsky proof planned here.

contents.name: Theorem 3.2.14 (moment criterion for tightness)
contents.reason: This sufficient condition for tightness belongs with the tightness theory of PT-7, where moment bounds can be stated with their appropriate weak-convergence consequences.

contents.name: Theorem 3.2.15 (subsequence criterion for weak convergence)
contents.reason: This metric-space subsequence criterion is different from the probability-convergence subsequence theorem built directly in this scaffold.

contents.name: Exercise 3.2.1 (weak convergence with nonconvergent densities)
contents.reason: The exercise distinguishes density convergence from weak convergence and naturally belongs with the later comparison of weak-convergence formulations.

contents.name: Exercise 3.2.2 Convergence of maxima
contents.reason: The extreme-value limit laws are a separate asymptotic-probability topic and would expand this general modes page into an unsupported tail-domain development.

contents.name: Exercise 3.2.3 (Gaussian maxima)
contents.reason: The Gaussian-maxima asymptotics are a specialized extreme-value calculation; they are not needed for any definition, implication, or counterexample in the present pair.

contents.name: Exercise 3.2.4 Fatou's lemma for weak convergence
contents.reason: This lower-semicontinuity integration result belongs with Portmanteau-style weak-convergence consequences, which the plan assigns to PT-7.

contents.name: Exercise 3.2.5 Integration to the limit
contents.reason: Its moment-controlled integration conclusion is weak-convergence theory beyond the finite-measure Vitali route used for L^1 convergence on this page.

contents.name: Exercise 3.2.6 The Levy Metric
contents.reason: The Levy metric metrizes distributional convergence and belongs with the future weak-convergence infrastructure, whereas d_0 here metrizes convergence in probability.

contents.name: Exercise 3.2.7 The Ky Fan metric
contents.reason: The exercise compares a probability-convergence metric with the Levy metric, a bridge best treated after both metric frameworks are available in PT-7.

contents.name: Exercise 3.2.8 (comparison of Ky Fan and beta metrics)
Exercise 3.2.9 (uniform CDF convergence for a continuous limit)
contents.reason: Uniform distribution-function convergence is a refinement of weak convergence at continuous limits, reserved for the later focused weak-convergence page.

contents.name: Exercise 3.2.10 (finite atomic approximation of a distribution)
contents.reason: Atomic approximation is a construction in the topology of distribution laws and therefore belongs to the planned weak-convergence and representation development.

contents.name: Exercise 3.2.11 (integer-valued weak convergence and point masses)
contents.reason: This discrete-law criterion is a special weak-convergence characterization and does not enter the selected real-random-variable implication proofs.

contents.name: Exercise 3.2.12, second assertion (distributional convergence to a constant implies probability)

EX 3.11, square-root spike specialization (L^1 but neither almost sure nor L^2)
THM 3.12 Implications: almost sure implies in probability
THM 3.12 Implications: L^p implies in probability
THM 3.12 Implications: L^r implies L^p for r at least p
THM 3.12 Implications: subsequence characterization of convergence in probability
THM 3.14 (continuous functions preserve convergence in probability)
1.4 Statement of laws of large numbers
contents.reason: This section announces the later laws-of-large-numbers agenda; it is read for context but its random-sum theorems are not prerequisites for the abstract modes development.

contents.name: THM 3.15 Strong law of large numbers
contents.reason: The iid strong-law statement is assigned to the planned strong-laws page, where the integrability hypothesis and proof methods can be developed without circularity.

contents.name: THM 3.16 Weak law of large numbers
contents.reason: The iid tail criterion is the later weak-laws page's central result; this pair supplies its convergence-in-probability vocabulary but does not duplicate the law.
